LITERARY NARRATIVE: In the selection below, a teenager helps during an apartment-building water outage.

When every faucet in Building C coughed air at once, Nia blamed Mr. Vale. He lived in the ground-floor apartment beside the utility room and had complained for weeks about people leaving the courtyard hose running. At the emergency meeting, he stood near the back holding a ring of keys, his expression so unsurprised that Nia mistook calm for satisfaction.

The property manager was across town. A plumber could not arrive until evening. Mr. Vale said the main valve was open, so the blockage must be elsewhere. Several residents answered at once, offering theories about the roof tank and the road repairs. Mr. Vale waited, then asked Nia whether she still made maps for the school newspaper. She said she did, though she did not see what that had to do with water.

He led her into the basement corridor. Pipes crossed the ceiling, disappearing behind walls and reappearing under stairwells. Their old labels had peeled away. Mr. Vale handed Nia a roll of blue tape and asked her to mark each branch while he tested valves. She drew the building as a set of boxes, adding lines wherever a pipe vanished. The work felt less like plumbing than tracing an argument whose middle sentences had been erased.

At the first valve, nothing changed. At the second, a pipe shuddered but remained silent. Nia heard residents upstairs opening taps after each test, then calling down the same answer. No water. Mr. Vale never rushed. He touched the pipes, listened, and wrote the result beside Nia's lines.

They found an unexpected branch behind a storage cabinet. Moving the cabinet revealed a narrow access panel painted the color of the wall. Inside, a valve handle sat halfway between open and closed. Nia reached for it, but Mr. Vale stopped her. If it fed the damaged laundry line, opening it could flood the basement. They needed evidence before motion.

Nia returned to the courtyard and compared apartment numbers with her map. The dry taps formed no simple vertical stack. Then a mother from the third floor mentioned that her kitchen tap had failed before her bathroom tap. That detail placed the interruption beyond the roof tank but before two branches separated. Nia circled the hidden valve.

Back downstairs, Mr. Vale turned it slowly while Nia watched the laundry pipe. It stayed dry. Above them came a distant thump, then a cheer traveling floor by floor as water reached the apartments. Someone must have brushed the handle while moving the cabinet days earlier, gradually narrowing the flow until sediment completed the blockage.

At the meeting that evening, residents praised Mr. Vale. He corrected them, pointing to Nia's map. She wanted to apologize for suspecting him, but the words seemed designed to make him comfort her. Instead, she asked why he had looked unsurprised that morning.

Mr. Vale lifted the key ring. He had managed a theater building years ago, he explained, and old buildings were always hiding one more route than their plans admitted. Surprise was expensive during an outage. Curiosity was more useful.

Nia taped a clean copy of the map inside the utility-room door. Beside the newly labeled valve, she added a note: Check before turning. Mr. Vale read it and nodded. The sentence applied to valves, she thought, but also to conclusions reached too quickly.

Before leaving, they walked the route once more. Nia added arrows showing normal flow and photographed each valve with its label visible. Mr. Vale suggested keeping the paper map too. A phone could lose power during the next emergency, and a diagram on the wall could be read by whoever arrived first. Their two records served the same facts under different conditions.

The following morning, Nia passed Mr. Vale in the courtyard. He was tightening the hose connection he had complained about. This time his concentrated expression did not seem accusing. She asked whether the map needed a line for the outdoor tap. He handed her the blue tape.
originality_notes: A problem-solving neighbor narrative about evidence and infrastructure; no courtship, orchestrated meeting, family approval, resistance, or commitment decision.
Independently composed for this replacement audit.
